---
title: "03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves"
---

## Why this topic matters

Ordinary sieves compute every value through $N$; summatory sieves compute only

$$F(N)=\sum_{n\le N}f(n)$$

when $N$ is too large to visit. Here “compute only” does not mean magically
skip information: it means find a recurrence whose arguments repeat among a
small set of floor quotients. The art is choosing the correct structure:

- **Du Jiao sieve:** an easy Dirichlet convolution isolates $F(N)$.
- **Min_25 sieve:** $f$ is multiplicative and $f(p)$ is a low-degree polynomial in $p$.
- **Powerful-number sieve:** remove an easy function agreeing with $f$ on primes, leaving support only on numbers whose prime exponents are never one.

Before this chapter, master multiplicative functions, Möbius inversion, and quotient grouping in [Chapter 02](../02-multiplicative-number-theory/chapter.qmd).

## Prerequisites and learning objectives

Read [multiplicative functions and divisor sums](../02-multiplicative-number-theory/chapter.qmd).
For weighted prefixes, the [discrete-sums chapter](../12-discrete-sums/chapter.qmd)
supplies polynomial block sums. You should learn to derive a prefix recurrence,
prove that its recursive states close under floor division, distinguish a
prime-sum sieve from full multiplicative enumeration, and justify a cutoff
using the actual time and storage model.

## Definitions and notation

$N\ge1$ is the fixed query bound. An arithmetic function $f$ has prefix
$F(x)=\sum_{1\le n\le x}f(n)$ for integer $x\ge0$, with $F(0)=0$.
$f*g$ means Dirichlet convolution. Coefficients lie in a commutative ring;
integer formulas are evaluated exactly before reduction unless their
denominators are units. In prime enumeration, $p_i$ is the $i$th prime
with zero-based index $p_0=2$. A cutoff $B$ is an integer preprocessing bound.
Operation counts below treat exact coefficient operations as constant time.

## 1. The $O(\sqrt{N})$ quotient-state space

Every recursive call in these methods should normally be one of the distinct
values $\lfloor N/i\rfloor$. This is a small state space because values below
$\sqrt N$ can occur directly, while every value above it equals $\lfloor N/i\rfloor$
for some $i<\sqrt N$. There are fewer than $2\sqrt N$ values in total. Two
common indexing schemes are:

- store large values in a hash map and precompute all values up to a cutoff;
- map $v$ to $v$ itself if $v≤\sqrt{N}$, otherwise to $N/v$ in a second array.

For $N=20$, the distinct states are $20,10,6,5,4,3,2,1$, rather than twenty
different arguments. This is the object being memoized; quotient grouping is
what makes a recurrence over all divisors practical.

Never accidentally memoize arbitrary arguments: that can turn an intended $O(\sqrt{N})$ state set into linear space.

Closure follows from the identity
$\lfloor\lfloor N/a\rfloor/b\rfloor=\lfloor N/(ab)\rfloor$ for positive
integers $a,b$: both sides count how many complete blocks of $ab$ fit in $N$.
Thus recursively dividing an existing quotient cannot create a new kind of
state. The map using a second array is injective on the *distinct large
quotients*: their producing indices are at most $\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$,
and different large quotient blocks have different right endpoints $N/v$.
This is a property of this state set, not of arbitrary integers $v$.

## 2. Du Jiao sieve from a convolution identity

Suppose $h=f*g$ and the prefixes of $h$ and $g$ are cheap. We want
$F(N)=\sum_{n\le N}f(n)$. Start by summing the *definition* of convolution:

$$H(N)=\sum_{n\le N}\sum_{d\mid n}f(n/d)g(d).$$

Writing $n=dk$ makes the meaning visible: for each possible $d$, the allowed
$k$ run through $1,\ldots,\lfloor N/d\rfloor$. Swapping those two sums gives

$$H(N)=\sum_{d\le N}g(d)F(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).$$

If $g(1)=1$, the $d=1$ term is exactly $F(N)$; move every other term to the
other side:

$$F(N)=H(N)-\sum_{d=2}^{N}g(d)F(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).$$

If instead $g(1)$ is another unit, divide the whole equation by $g(1)$ after
isolating $g(1)F(N)$; without an invertible $g(1)$ this recurrence is not an
algorithmic contract. Commutativity lets you swap the names of $f,g$ if the
other factor has easier prefix sums. The remaining formula appears to have $N$ terms, but all indices
$\lfloor N/d\rfloor$ repeat. Group a block $l\le d\le r$ with one quotient $q$;
its total coefficient is $G(r)-G(l-1)$. That quotient grouping is the speedup,
not the recurrence alone.

### Mertens and totient prefixes

Let $M(N)=\sum_{n\le N}\mu(n)$. The identity $\mu*1=\varepsilon$ says that
the convolution prefix $H(N)$ is $1$ for every $N\ge1$. Here $g=1$, so a block
of indices $[l,r]$ has coefficient $r-l+1$. Substitution gives

$$
M(N)=1-\sum_{l\in\mathcal B_N}
(r_N(l)-l+1)M(\lfloor N/l\rfloor),
\qquad r_N(l)=\left\lfloor\frac{N}{\lfloor N/l\rfloor}\right\rfloor.
$$

Here $\mathcal B_N$ is the set of quotient-block starts: begin with $l=2$ and
repeatedly replace $l$ by $r_N(l)+1$. It is not the set of every integer from
$2$ through $N$.

Let $\Phi(N)=\sum_{n\le N}\varphi(n)$. The identity
$\varphi*1=\operatorname{id}$ says its convolution prefix is
$1+2+\cdots+N=T(N)=N(N+1)/2$, giving

$$
\Phi(N)=T(N)-\sum_{l\in\mathcal B_N}
(r_N(l)-l+1)\Phi(\lfloor N/l\rfloor),
$$

with the same definitions of $\mathcal B_N$ and $r_N(l)$.

Precompute through $B\ge\sqrt N$ and memoize only larger quotient states.
Such a state is $x=\lfloor N/k\rfloor$ for $k\le N/B$.
Its quotient loop takes $O(\sqrt x)$ operations, so all memoized work is at most

$$
O\left(\sum_{k\le N/B}\sqrt{N/k}\right)
=O\left(\sqrt N\sqrt{N/B}\right)
=O(N/\sqrt B).
$$

The middle bound follows by comparing $\sum_{k\le K}k^{-1/2}$ with its
integral, which is at most $2\sqrt K$ up to a constant.
Total time is $O(B+N/\sqrt B)$ and storage is $O(B+N/B)$, assuming
$O(1)$ prefix access and memo lookup. Choosing $B$ near $N^{2/3}$
balances the terms and gives $O(N^{2/3})$ time and space for one query.
This bound does not automatically amortize across unrelated query bounds.

**Worked recurrence.** For $N=6$, $\mu(1),\ldots,\mu(6)$ are
$1,-1,-1,0,-1,1$. The block formula uses $[2,2],[3,3],[4,6]$:
$M(6)=1-M(3)-M(2)-3M(1)=1-(-1)-0-3=-1$.
The corresponding totient formula gives
$\Phi(6)=21-\Phi(3)-\Phi(2)-3\Phi(1)=21-4-2-3=12$.
The weights are lengths of blocks, not numbers of distinct quotient values.

The quadratic scale of $\sum\varphi(n)$ requires wide intermediates. Reduce modulo the problem modulus inside every operation if that is what the statement asks.

### Derivation workflow

1. Name the wanted prefix $F$.
2. Find $g$ so $h=f*g$ has an elementary prefix.
3. Sum $h(n)$ for $n≤N$, swap $n=dk$, and isolate $F(N)$.
4. Express coefficient sums on $[l,r]$ with prefix formulas.
5. Confirm every recursive argument is $\lfloor N/l\rfloor$ and smaller than $N$.

## 3. Prime-sum sieve: the engine inside Min_25

Min_25 first solves a narrower problem: quickly find sums over primes, such as
$\sum_{p\le w}p^k$, at every quotient state $w=\lfloor N/l\rfloor$. Initialize

$$g_k(w)=\sum_{i=2}^{w}i^{k}.$$

At the start, $g_k(w)$ is the sum over **all** integers $2,\ldots,w$. Process
primes $p$ in increasing order. At the $p$ stage, subtract the composites whose
smallest prime factor is $p$; for every state $w\ge p^2$ this is

$$g_k(w)\mathrel{-}=p^{k}\left(g_k(\lfloor w/p\rfloor)-S_k(p-1)\right),$$

where $S_k(p-1)=\sum_{q<p,q prime}q^{k}$. After processing all $p≤\sqrt{N}$, $g_k(w)=\sum_{q≤w,q prime}q^{k}$.

Why $p^2$? Any composite first removed at this stage has least prime factor
$p$, hence it is $p\cdot x$ with $x\ge p$. Just before the $p$ stage,
$g_k(\lfloor w/p\rfloor)$ consists of two kinds of surviving entries: primes below $p$, which
are deliberately retained as final prime answers, and integers having no prime
factor below $p$. Only the second kind can be a valid cofactor $x$, so
$S_k(p-1)$ removes the retained small primes. Updating states in descending
order prevents the right side from using values already modified by the
current prime. After all relevant stages, only prime contributions remain.

**Worked sieve.** For $k=0,N=10$, initially $g_0(10)=9$, counting $2,\ldots,10$.
The $p=2$ update removes $4,6,8,10$, leaving five entries. The $p=3$
update removes $9$, leaving the four primes $2,3,5,7$.
At $w=5$, processing prime two before $w=10$ would change the cofactor
data used by larger states; descending order is what preserves the stage invariant.

For $k=0$ this computes $\pi(w)$, the number of primes at most $w$.
One array uses $O(\sqrt N)$ space. An elementary upper bound on update count
is $O(N^{3/4})$: primes at most $N^{1/4}$ have at most $2\sqrt N$ states
each, while larger primes can update only $O(N/p^2)$ large states;
$N\sum_{j>N^{1/4}}j^{-2}=O(N^{3/4})$.
Using prime-density estimates sharpens this to
$O(N^{3/4}/\log N)$ asymptotically for this prime-sum core, as discussed in the
[official ABC370 editorial](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc370/editorial/10906?lang=en).
The simple bound already explains why the prime-sum stage is sublinear.

## 4. Full Min_25 sieve

Min_25 extends that prime-sum engine to a multiplicative function. Assume $f$
is multiplicative, each $f(p^{e})$ is computable in $O(1)$, and the *prime*
values, not necessarily all prime-power values, satisfy

$$f(p)=\sum_{k=0}^{K}c_kp^{k}$$

for small fixed $K$. Run the prime-sum sieve for each required power $k$; combine the arrays to obtain

$$G_f(x)=\sum_{p\le x}f(p).$$

The prime-sum sieve gives the contribution of prime numbers. To cover every
composite exactly once, enumerate it by its **least** prime and the exact
exponent of that prime. Index primes from $p_0=2$ and set
$G_f(p_{-1})=0$. Define $S(x,y)$ as the sum of $f(n)$ for $2\le n\le x$
whose least prime is at least $p_y$. Calls maintain $p_{y-1}\le x$ (with the
$y=0$ sentinel understood), so its prime-only base contribution is
$G_f(x)-G_f(p_{y-1})$ and is zero when the interval contains no prime.
For every possible least prime $p_i$, enumerate an exponent $e\ge1$. The term
with $S$ counts numbers $p_i^e m$ where $m>1$ has no prime factor at most $p_i$;
the separate term counts pure powers (the prime $p_i$ itself is already in the
base term):

$$
S(x,y)=G_f(x)-G_f(p_{y-1})+
\sum_{\substack{i\ge y\\p_i^2\le x}}
\sum_{\substack{e\ge1\\p_i^{e+1}\le x}}
\left(f(p_i^e)S(\lfloor x/p_i^e\rfloor,i+1)+f(p_i^{e+1})\right).
$$

Finally $f(1)+S(N,0)=1+S(N,0)$ is the prefix, using the standard convention for
a multiplicative function. The shift in the pure-power exponent is deliberate:
as $e=1,2,\ldots$, those terms list $p_i^2,p_i^3,\ldots$ exactly once, while the
cofactor term uses $p_i^e$ as the exact valuation. The condition
$p_i^{e+1}\le x$ also safely ends the cofactor branch: any permitted nontrivial
cofactor is at least $p_{i+1}>p_i$. This decomposition is unique.

As a hand check, take $f(n)=1$ and $x=10$. The base term counts the four primes
$2,3,5,7$. The branch for least prime $2$ contributes $6,10$ from
$2\cdot\{3,5\}$ and the pure powers $4,8$; the branch for least prime $3$
contributes the pure power $9$. Together with $f(1)$ these are all ten integers,
each assigned to exactly one least-prime branch.

Keep the enumeration cost separate from the prime-sum cost. Let $E(N)$ be
the number of $(i,e)$ branches actually visited by the displayed recursion
from $(N,0)$. With $O(1)$ local values and prime-prefix access, the cost is
$O((K+1)N^{3/4}+E(N))$ by the elementary prime-stage bound, with
$O((K+1)\sqrt N+\log N)$ storage for arrays and a depth-first stack.
The logarithmic stack bound follows because each recursive step divides by
at least two. A conservative $E(N)=O(N)$ bound follows by assigning each
call its product of selected prime powers: the strictly increasing prime
indices give a unique factorization path for every product, and all products
are at most $N$. Practical enumeration is much smaller on common instances,
but this is not a proof that every variant inherits the prime-sum bound.
Count these branches when benchmarking the chosen library; optimized Min_25
variants require their own complexity analysis.

**Applicability signals.** $N$ is around $10^{9}–10^{12}$, the statement gives a multiplicative function through its prime powers, and its value at a prime is polynomial (examples: $\varphi(p)=p-1$, $\mu(p)=-1$, $\sigma_k(p)=1+p^{k}$).

**Non-applicable cases.** If $f(p)$ depends on an arbitrary property of $p$ for which no fast prime prefix exists, standard Min_25 has no base data. If only $\mu/\varphi$ prefixes are needed, Du Jiao is simpler.

## 5. Powerful-number support

A positive integer is powerful if every prime dividing it has exponent at least
two. For example, $72=2^3\cdot3^2$ is powerful whereas $12=2^2\cdot3$ is not.
The count through $N$ is $O(\sqrt N)$ because every powerful integer has the
unique representation

$$n=a^2b^3,\qquad b\text{ square-free}.$$

For each prime exponent $e\ge2$, choose the unique
$e=2u+3v$ with $v\in\{0,1\}$; the primes with $v=1$ form $b$. Consequently
$b\le N^{1/3}$ and $a\le\sqrt{N/b^3}$. Summing over $b$ gives
$\sqrt N\sum_b b^{-3/2}=O(\sqrt N)$ candidates. The requirement that $b$ be
square-free is what makes the representation unique.

This sparsity yields another generic strategy. Choose an easy multiplicative
$g$ agreeing with $f$ on primes, and define

$$h=f*g^{-1}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f=h*g.$$

Because multiplicative functions have value $1$ at $1$, the prime-power
convolution identity gives $h(p)=f(p)-g(p)=0$. Multiplicativity then forces
$h(n)=0$ whenever any prime has exponent exactly one: its product over
prime-power factors contains $h(p)=0$. Thus $h$ is supported on powerful
numbers. Let $G(x)=\sum_{n\le x}g(n)$. In the convolution $f=h*g$, choosing a
divisor $d$ for the $h$ factor leaves a $g$ factor through $\lfloor N/d\rfloor$;
summing those choices gives

$$F(N)=\sum_{d\le N\atop d\text{ powerful}}h(d)G(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).$$

Compute local prime-power coefficients from

$$f(p^{e})=\sum_{j=0}^{e}h(p^{j})g(p^{e-j}),$$

so $h(1)=1$, $h(p)=0$, and for $e≥2$,

$$h(p^{e})=f(p^{e})-\sum_{j=0}^{e-1}h(p^{j})g(p^{e-j}).$$

Enumerate powerful numbers by DFS over increasing primes, choosing exponent zero or at least two; accumulate $h(d)G(N/d)$. Prune when $d·p²>N$. Alternatively enumerate the unique $a²b³$ representation when the coefficient is easier to recover that way.

This method is attractive when $G(x)$ is elementary or already available and $h(p^{e})$ is cheap. Complexity is commonly around $O(\sqrt{N} \operatorname{polylog} N)$ plus the cost of obtaining $G$ and primes, but must be derived for the exact enumeration.

### A common special case: perfect powers

To count integers $n>1$ representable as $a^{b}$ with $a,b>1$, enumerate exponents but
remove duplicate representations. If
$n=\prod_i p_i^{e_i}$, its maximal possible exponent is $\gcd_i e_i$; thus $n$
is a nontrivial perfect power exactly when this gcd exceeds one. Möbius inversion
over exponents, or counting by the maximal exponent, avoids double counting.
Integer kth roots must be corrected with exact 128-bit power comparisons—floating-
point `pow` alone is unsafe near $10^{18}$.

### Worked powerful-support transformation

Let $f(n)=\tau(n)$ and $g(n)=2^{\omega(n)}$, where $\omega(n)$ counts
distinct prime factors. Both functions equal two at a prime. At $p^e$,
$g(p^e)=2$ for $e\ge1$. Local convolution gives
$h(p)=0$, $h(p^2)=3-2=1$, and
$h(p^3)=4-(2+0+2)=0$. Continuing gives $h(p^{2j})=1$
and $h(p^{2j+1})=0$: the local generating-series quotient is

$$
\frac{\sum_{e\ge0}(e+1)t^e}{1+2t+2t^2+\cdots}
=\frac{1/(1-t)^2}{(1+t)/(1-t)}
=\frac1{1-t^2}.
$$

These are formal identities with constant-one denominators, valid over the
integers without dividing coefficients. Thus $h$ is the indicator of squares,
and $\sum_{n\le N}\tau(n)=\sum_{a\le\sqrt N}G(\lfloor N/a^2\rfloor)$.
This is an identity, not automatically a fast algorithm: we still need cheap
$G$. Matching on primes makes support sparse but does not supply that prefix.
For $N=4$, $G(4)=1+2+2+2=7$ and $G(1)=1$, giving $8$.

## 6. Choosing a method

| Signal | First choice | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| known simple $f*g=h$ | Du Jiao | shortest recurrence, quotient memoization |
| polynomial $f(p)$ and arbitrary manageable $f(p^{e})$ | Min_25 | sieves prime contributions then enumerates least primes |
| can match $f(p)$ with an easy $g$; differences begin at $p²$ | powerful-number sieve | transformed support is sparse |
| only prime count/sums are wanted | prime-sum core | no full multiplicative DFS needed |

## Pitfalls

- Prove the convolution identity before optimizing it; a swapped divisor argument silently computes the wrong function.
- In prime-sum DP, process $w$ descending and only while $w≥p²$.
- Distinguish “primes $<p$” from “primes $≤p$” in the base subtraction.
- Min_25 recursion must enforce strictly increasing prime factors after choosing the least prime.
- Include $f(1)$ exactly once.
- Use 128-bit arithmetic for $p²$, prime-power growth, polynomial sums, and unmodded answers.
- Modular polynomial sums may require division by $2,6,…$; use integer formulas before reduction if the modulus is not guaranteed coprime to denominators.
- Cached values keyed by the actual argument $x$ may be reused across queries
  for the same function and coefficient ring. Array slots keyed by $N/x$
  are query-specific and must be rebuilt when $N$ changes.

## Ordered practice

### 1. [Relatively Prime Powers](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1036/F) — Codeforces 1036F

- **Level:** Mastery · **Language:** English/Russian
- **Trains:** perfect-power counting, Möbius inversion over exponents, exact integer roots.
- **Editorial:** [official Educational Round 50 editorial](https://codeforces.com/blog/entry/61727)

<details><summary>Hint 1</summary>Count numbers that are not expressible as a nontrivial perfect power, then complement.</details>
<details><summary>Hint 2</summary>A number may appear under several exponents; classify it by the gcd of exponents in its prime factorization.</details>
<details><summary>Hint 3</summary>Use Möbius inclusion–exclusion on exponents and exact corrected kth roots up to the relevant logarithm.</details>

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Editorial guidance: many queries"}
The exponent-inversion formula derives the answer, but the official task has
many queries. Precompute all non-square perfect powers through the maximum
query: enumerate bases for odd exponents $3,5,\ldots,\lfloor\log_2 X\rfloor$,
discard squares using exact integer square roots, then sort and deduplicate.
Every non-square perfect power has an odd exponent at least three in some
representation. The largest base range is the cube range, $X^{1/3}$;
the total candidates are $O(X^{1/3}\log X)$ by a conservative bound.
For each query $n$, squares contribute $\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor-1$ and a
binary search counts precomputed non-squares. The elegant count is
$n-\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor-C(n)$. Exact roots and deduplication matter:
$64$ has several representations but is removed as a square.
:::

### 2. [A Simple Math Problem](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P3768) — Luogu P3768

- **Level:** Capstone · **Language:** Chinese
- **Prerequisites:** totient convolution, Du Jiao sieve, polynomial block sums.
- **Editorial:** [Luogu solution index (Chinese; login required)](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/solution/P3768). A complete local reduction is in [the capstone guide](../13-capstones/chapter.qmd).

<details><summary>Hint 1</summary>Rewrite the gcd-weighted double sum by extracting the gcd and using a totient identity.</details>
<details><summary>Hint 2</summary>The remaining expression needs prefix sums of a weighted totient function, not plain $\varphi$.</details>
<details><summary>Hint 3</summary>Derive its convolution recurrence, evaluate polynomial coefficients over quotient blocks, and reduce throughout modulo the given large prime. The exact-integer derivation also works for composite answer moduli if no invalid modular division is introduced.</details>

## Exercises with solutions

### 1. Blocks and boundary cases — concept check

List the quotient blocks for $N=10$, then compute $M(10)$ from smaller
Mertens prefixes.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint and solution"}
Starting at two, the blocks are $[2,2],[3,3],[4,5],[6,10]$, with
quotients $5,3,2,1$. Since $M(5)=-2,M(3)=-1,M(2)=0,M(1)=1$,
$M(10)=1-(-2)-(-1)-2\cdot0-5=-1$.
At $N=1$ there are no blocks and $M(1)=1$.
:::

### 2. A weighted recurrence — derivation

Let $f(n)=n^2\varphi(n)$. Find a convolution with an elementary prefix,
and write the grouped recurrence for $F(N)$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint and solution"}
Take $g(n)=n^2$. Then
$(f*g)(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d^2\varphi(d)(n/d)^2
=n^2\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n^3$.
Thus $F(N)=\sum_{n\le N}n^3-
\sum_{[l,r],\,l\ge2}(\sum_{d=l}^r d^2)F(\lfloor N/l\rfloor)$.
Here $\sum_{n\le N}n^3=[N(N+1)/2]^2$; square sums provide block weights.
At $N=3$, $F(3)=1+4+18=23=36-4-9$.
All fractions in power-sum formulas are exact integer divisions if the
answer modulus does not permit the corresponding inverses.
:::

### 3. Perfect powers without duplicates — synthesis

Count the integers $2\le n\le X$ that are nontrivial perfect powers,
using exact integer roots and Möbius values of exponents.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint and solution"}
If the gcd of the prime exponents of $n$ is $g$, then $n$ is an $e$th
power iff $e\mid g$. The weight
$-\sum_{e\mid g,\,e\ge2}\mu(e)$ is zero when $g=1$ and one otherwise.
Summing by $e$ gives

$$-\sum_{e=2}^{\lfloor\log_2 X\rfloor}
\mu(e)\left(\lfloor X^{1/e}\rfloor-1\right).$$

Subtract one to exclude base one. At $X=16$, the terms are
$3+1+0=4$, representing $4,8,9,16$. Each root may be found by binary
search with capped integer powers; one safe baseline uses
$O(\log X\log\log X)$ arithmetic operations per root and $O(\log X)$
roots. A faster integer-root library must still correct rounding exactly.
:::

## Summary and reference sheet

The closed state set is $\{\lfloor N/i\rfloor:1\le i\le N\}$.
Du Jiao isolates a prefix from $h=f*g$ when $g(1)$ is a unit and the
other prefixes are cheap; one-query cost is $O(B+N/\sqrt B)$ for
$B\ge\sqrt N$. Prime-sum sieving removes composites at their unique
least-prime stage and updates quotient values downward.
Full multiplicative enumeration additionally chooses the exact least-prime
exponent; its branch count is a separate cost.
Matching functions on primes confines their convolution quotient to powerful
numbers, but a cheap prefix for the matched function remains essential.
Every method must include the value at one exactly once.
